explain.why: Sesudah bagian kosong ada kata benda “name”. Jadi pakai “Her”.
explain.rule: Kata ganti subjek jadi subjek. Kata ganti objek berdiri sesudah kata kerja. Kata kepemilikan kayak her berdiri sebelum kata benda. Hers berdiri sendiri.
explain.memory: “Her name”, tapi “the name is hers”.
explain.avoid: Tulis bentuk lengkapnya, jangan hanya kata dasarnya.

items.sentence: The teacher walks in and says: “___ your books to page 40, everyone.”

distractors.misconception: adding -s as if the command needed subject-verb agreement with a singular subject
using the -ing form on its own, which describes an activity instead of telling someone to act
using a to-infinitive where a direct command is required

explain.why: Gurunya lagi nyuruh seisi kelas buat buka buku sekarang, jadi perintahnya mulai dari bentuk dasar: “Open your books.”
explain.rule: Kalimat perintah pakai kata kerja bentuk dasar aja: tanpa subjek, tanpa -s, tanpa -ing, dan tanpa “to” di depan.
explain.memory: Perintah itu polosan: “Open”, “Sit”, “Listen”.
explain.avoid: Kalau kalimatnya nyuruh orang ngelakuin sesuatu, mulai dari kata kerja polos tanpa embel-embel.

items.sentence: My sister ___ tea after dinner; she never skips it.

distractors.misconception: moves the adverb between the verb and its object, copying Indonesian word order
leaving the bare verb with no third-person marking after a singular subject
inserting 'is' before a main verb, blending the 'be' pattern with the present simple

explain.why: “Always” duduk sebelum kata kerja utama, dan “drinks” tetap pakai -s buat orang ketiga tunggal: “My sister always drinks tea.”
explain.rule: Kata frekuensi (“always”, “usually”, “often”, “never”) duduk sebelum kata kerja utama, dan kata kerjanya tetap nyocokin subjek.
explain.memory: Frekuensi dulu, kata kerja belakangan: “She always drinks”.
explain.avoid: Selipkan kata frekuensi pas sebelum kata kerja utama, terus cek akhiran kata kerjanya ke subjek.

items.sentence: Is this ___ bag? She was sitting here a minute ago.

distractors.misconception: drops the marker of ownership entirely, lining up two nouns as Indonesian does
writes a plain -s ending that superficially resembles the possessive but loses the apostrophe
inserting a duplicate owner pronoun after the name, marking possession twice

explain.why: Tanda kepemilikan nempel di nama pemiliknya: “Sinta's bag” artinya tas itu punya Sinta.
explain.rule: Buat bilang sesuatu punya seseorang, tambahin apostrof + s ke namanya dan taruh sebelum barangnya: “Sinta's bag”.
explain.memory: Pemilik + apostrof s + barang: “Sinta's bag”.
explain.avoid: Tanya siapa pemiliknya, tambahin apostrof + s ke nama itu, dan buang kata ganti tambahan.

items.sentence: At the café counter, the barista asks what you want. You say: “I ___ a glass of orange juice, please.”

distractors.misconception: stating a general preference in casual flat form instead of the polite request formula
forcing a stative desire verb into the progressive to sound ongoing
gluing an -ing onto the verb after 'would', a blend of two separate patterns

explain.why: Mesen dengan sopan pakai “would like”: “I would like a glass of orange juice, please.”
explain.rule: “Would like” + kata benda dipakai buat minta sesuatu dengan sopan saat ini; “like” polos cuma nyatain selera umum.
explain.memory: Pesenan sopan: “I would like ..., please.”
explain.avoid: Kalau minta sesuatu dengan sopan, pakai “would like” dan biarin kata kerja sesudah “would” tetap dasar.

items.sentence: My brother ___ up early on Sundays, so he never sets an alarm before the weekend.

distractors.misconception: following the feeling verb with a bare infinitive, chaining verbs directly as Indonesian does
mixes the to-infinitive and the -ing ending into one broken shape
inserting 'is' before the feeling verb, a hybrid of the adjective pattern and a normal verb

explain.why: Sesudah kata kerja perasaan kayak “hates”, kegiatannya pakai -ing: “hates getting up early”.
explain.rule: “Like”, “love”, “hate”, dan “enjoy” diikuti kata kerja + -ing kalau ngomongin kegiatan secara umum.
explain.memory: Perasaan doyan -ing: “love swimming”, “hate waiting”.
explain.avoid: Sesudah “like”, “love”, atau “hate”, ubah kegiatan berikutnya jadi bentuk -ing.

items.sentence: “Have you ever ___ to Japan?” “No, never, but I really want to go.”

distractors.misconception: using the past-simple form inside a present perfect question frame
leaving the bare verb although 'have' needs the past participle after it
mixes 'have' with a finite past form of 'be' instead of the participle

explain.why: “Have you ever” nanyain pengalaman hidup, dan sesudah “have” kata kerjanya wajib past participle: “been”.
explain.rule: Present perfect dengan “ever” dan “never” ngomongin pengalaman sampai sekarang: “have/has” + past participle.
explain.memory: “Ever” jalannya bareng “have been”, “have seen”, “have done”.
explain.avoid: Sesudah “have” atau “has”, selalu ambil bentuk ketiga kata kerjanya, jangan past simple.

items.sentence: We ___ in this flat since 2019, and we still love it here.

distractors.misconception: using the plain present as a habit statement, ignoring the stretch of time that began in the past
choosing the present progressive for right now, though the span from 2019 needs a past-to-present link
sealing the period off as a completed event, though the family still lives there

explain.why: “Since 2019” plus “we still love it” artinya tinggalnya mulai dulu dan masih lanjut, jadi “have lived” yang pas.
explain.rule: Buat keadaan yang mulai di masa lalu dan masih bener, pakai present perfect dengan “for” (lama waktu) atau “since” (titik mulai).
explain.memory: “Since 2019” narik kata kerjanya jadi “have lived”.
explain.avoid: Lihat “since” atau “for” dengan sesuatu yang masih bener? Sambungin masa lalu ke sekarang pakai “have/has” + participle.

items.sentence: I wish I ___ closer to the office; the commute eats two hours of my day.

distractors.misconception: keeping the present tense after 'wish', reading the situation as a real current fact
inserting 'would' for the speaker's own situation, as if the sentence were a result clause
reaching two steps back with the past perfect, aiming the wish at a finished past moment

explain.why: Harapan soal sekarang pakai past simple buat nandain ketidaknyataan: “I wish I lived closer.”
explain.rule: “Wish/if only” + past simple nyatain keadaan sekarang yang pengin kamu ubah.
explain.memory: Harapan soal sekarang = mundur satu langkah: “wish I lived”.
explain.avoid: Berharap soal sekarang? Mundurin kata kerjanya satu langkah: bentuk sekarang jadi past simple.

items.sentence: If only I ___ the contract more carefully before signing it last year.

distractors.misconception: staying with the past simple, which cannot mark the unreal past that regret needs
moving the 'would have' shape of the result clause into the wish clause itself
choosing the present perfect, which ties the missed reading to the present moment

explain.why: Penyesalan soal kejadian lampau yang selesai pakai past perfect: “If only I had read the contract.”
explain.rule: “Wish/if only” + past perfect nengok ke kejadian lampau yang udah nggak bisa diubah.
explain.memory: Penyesalan lampau = “if only I had ...”.
explain.avoid: Nyeselin sesuatu yang udah lewat? Mundur dua langkah: past perfect sesudah “if only”.

items.sentence: You ___ the news by now — the memo about the merger went to every department on Monday morning.

distractors.misconception: reading 'by now' as a point still ahead and choosing a plain prediction about the future
forcing the verb into the present progressive although 'by now' asks for an accumulated result
picking the future continuous for an event the timeline treats as already delivered

explain.why: “By now” ngiket dugaannya ke saat ini: “will have heard” yakin banget kabar itu udah sampai.
explain.rule: “Will have” + past participle bisa nyatain dugaan yakin kalau sesuatu udah selesai, apalagi ada penanda kayak “by now”.
explain.memory: “You'll have heard by now” = aku yakin kabarnya udah sampai.
explain.avoid: Pas “will” ketemu penanda kayak “by now”, cek dulu: ini nebak fakta yang udah selesai, atau ngeramal?

items.sentence: The painting is believed ___ from the gallery during the postwar chaos, decades before it resurfaced in Vienna.

distractors.misconception: using the simple passive shape, hiding that the theft was a prior event seen from the report
choosing the active infinitive, which would make the painting the one who stole
attaching a gerund where the reporting verb 'believe' takes the to-infinitive pattern

explain.why: Pencuriannya kejadian puluhan tahun sebelum keyakinan hari ini, dan lukisannya jadi sasarannya, jadi “to have been stolen” bawa dua sinyal itu sekaligus.
explain.rule: Sesudah kata pelaporan kayak “is believed/said/thought”, pakai “to have been” + past participle buat kejadian lebih awal yang menimpa subjeknya.
explain.memory: Lebih dulu + pasif = “to have been stolen”.
explain.avoid: Tanya dua hal: kejadiannya lebih dulu? subjeknya yang kena? Dua-duanya iya berarti “to have been done”.

items.sentence: The board formally demanded that the director ___ before the audit results were made public.

distractors.misconception: applying ordinary subject-verb agreement with a singular subject inside the demand clause
backshifting the verb as ordinary reported speech instead of keeping the base subjunctive
softening the demand with a conditional 'would', as if the clause reported a hypothetical

explain.why: Sesudah “demanded that”, kata kerja di dalamnya tetap subjunctive dasar apa pun subjek dan waktunya: “that the director resign”.
explain.rule: Kata kerja tuntutan dan usulan (“demand”, “insist”, “suggest”, “require”) bawa klausa “that” dengan bentuk dasar: “demand that she resign”.
explain.memory: Tuntutan nelanjangin kata kerja: “demand that he resign”.
explain.avoid: Sesudah “demand/insist/suggest” + “that”, bekuin kata kerjanya di bentuk kamus, apa pun subjek dan waktu di sekitarnya.

items.sentence: The shipment arrived nine days late, ___ forced the plant to halt its assembly line.

distractors.misconception: using 'what' as a relative pronoun, though it cannot point back to an antecedent
using 'that' to add extra detail after a comma, though it only opens essential clauses
starting a fresh pronoun clause and splicing two sentences together in a non-standard join

explain.why: Yang maksa pabrik berhenti itu keterlambatannya, alias seluruh klausa pertama, dan cuma “which” yang bisa mungut klausa utuh sesudah koma.
explain.rule: Klausa relatif sentensial pakai “, which” buat komentarin seluruh pernyataan sebelumnya, bukan cuma satu kata benda.
explain.memory: Komentarin semuanya? Koma + “which”.
explain.avoid: Kalau komentarnya soal seluruh pernyataan sebelumnya, taruh koma plus “which”; nggak ada kata lain yang muat di slot itu.

items.sentence: Where is Tom? I can't see ___.

distractors.misconception: subject-pronoun-in-object-position
possessive-form-as-person-object
subject-pronoun-and-gender-mismatch

items.sentence: I bought a book and a pen yesterday. ___ book is very interesting.

distractors.misconception: first-mention article reused
vowel-article before consonant sound
plural-or-uncountable quantifier

items.sentence: Look at ___ photo in my hand — it is from our holiday.

distractors.misconception: correctly matching singular but ignoring the nearness cue
correctly matching nearness but ignoring singular agreement
using a plural far demonstrative with a singular, near noun

items.sentence: Mr. and Mrs. Lee live next door. ___ house is very big.

distractors.misconception: subject pronoun
possessive pronoun
object pronoun

items.sentence: ___ you got a pen I can borrow?

distractors.misconception: third-person-form transfer
do-support with have got
be-verb substitution

items.sentence: The cat is ___ the bed, so we cannot see it.

distractors.misconception: surface-reading despite hidden cue
point-location-overuse
movement-preposition-substitution

items.sentence: ___ does the movie start? — At seven o'clock.

distractors.misconception: thing-question substitution
place-question substitution
person-question substitution

items.sentence: ___ your parents at home last night?

distractors.misconception: singular-past transfer
do-support added to a be question
present-tense substitution

items.sentence: We bought ___ bananas at the market this morning.

distractors.misconception: applies a singular indefinite article to a plural noun
applies a singular indefinite article to a plural noun and ignores the consonant sound
applies the uncountable-noun quantifier to a countable plural noun

items.sentence: My sister ___ the bus to work every day, so she knows the timetable by heart.

distractors.misconception: Assumes present time always requires present continuous.
missing subject-verb agreement / bare form
past tense used for a timeless fact

items.sentence: The bus is free for students, so you ___ pay for a ticket.

distractors.misconception: treats 'mustn't' as the negation of obligation rather than prohibition
confuses lack of requirement with lack of permission/ability
confuses absence of necessity with negative advice

items.sentence: If you finish your homework tonight, we ___ a film together.

distractors.misconception: drops the future marker entirely, defaulting to present simple
real condition treated as hypothetical
uses simple past for an explicitly future consequence

items.sentence: Of the five hotels we compared, this one is ___.

distractors.misconception: comparative used for a ranking within a group of three or more
applies the periphrastic 'more + adjective' pattern to a short one-syllable adjective that takes '-er'
base adjective used without comparative marking

items.sentence: Sara was walking home when it suddenly ___ to rain.

distractors.misconception: aspect confusion (progressive for a single completed trip)
present-tense substitution
confuses interrupted past action with present perfect result

items.sentence: There isn't ___ time before the flight, so pack quickly.

distractors.misconception: countable-quantity-substitution
positive-quantifier-in-negative
singular-article-with-uncountable

items.sentence: The sequel is fun, but it is ___ the first film — the first one still makes people laugh more.

distractors.misconception: reverses the direction of the comparison stated in the context
keeps the plain equality frame although the context states a clear difference
mixes the equality frame 'as ... as' with comparative 'than'

items.sentence: They walked ___ the beach for an hour, keeping the sea on their right the whole time.

distractors.misconception: uses the side-to-side crossing preposition for movement that follows a line
uses the enclosed-space movement preposition for a path along an open line
uses the above-and-across preposition for movement following a line, not over an obstacle

items.sentence: She has worked at that small clinic ___ 2021, when she moved back to her hometown.

distractors.misconception: Applies duration preposition 'for' to a point-in-time event rather than a length of time.
uses the within-a-period preposition 'during' where a starting point needs 'since'
Uses the conjunction 'while' where a preposition is grammatically required before a noun phrase.

items.sentence: A: I met one of your neighbours at the market this morning. B: Oh, really? ___ exactly?

distractors.misconception: reads an object question as a subject question, reversing who did what
drops the auxiliary 'did' required in an object question
Adds 'did' and keeps the past-tense main verb form together.

items.sentence: I ___ three cups of coffee today, and the day isn't over yet.

distractors.misconception: closes an unfinished time period with the past simple
over-applies continuous aspect whenever a time span like 'this year' appears
states a completed-so-far count with the plain present simple

items.sentence: Which completion shows a plan decided before the moment of speaking? 'We ___ my cousins in Lombok next month — we booked the flights last week.'

distractors.misconception: uses the moment-of-speaking decision form for a plan made before speaking
uses the timetable present simple for a personal plan
structural error: double -ing after 'going to'

items.sentence: Which option expresses the strongest positive deduction supported by the evidence? The kitchen smells of garlic and I can hear pans clattering, so Dad ___ be cooking dinner.

distractors.misconception: using 'can' for a specific present possibility about one situation
confuses the polarity of the deduction
deduction confused with expectation/advice

items.sentence: Even from the back row, we ___ hear every note at the concert last night.

distractors.misconception: uses present-tense modal for a clearly past narrative
adds 'to' after a modal that takes the bare infinitive
present-tense substitution

items.sentence: You ___ tell anyone about the surprise party — it has to stay a secret until Saturday.

distractors.misconception: reads a prohibition as mere absence of necessity
treating general advice modal as equally strong as urgent-consequence modal
Uses the past/tentative form of 'can' for a present-tense rule.

items.sentence: We'll have the picnic in the park tomorrow unless it ___.

distractors.misconception: carries the negative verb over from the 'if it doesn't rain' version instead of letting 'unless' supply the negation
stacks both a future 'will' and a negative inside the condition clause after 'unless'
uses future 'will' inside a condition clause because the picnic itself is in the future

items.sentence: We visited a small farm last weekend, and ___ animals we saw there were very friendly.

distractors.misconception: extends the zero-article-for-plurals rule to a plural noun that context has already made specific
applies a singular indefinite article to a plural noun
applies a singular indefinite article to a plural noun and ignores that the noun is already specific

items.sentence: My sister is really good at ___ with difficult customers without losing her temper.

distractors.misconception: inserts a to-infinitive right after the preposition 'at', treating every verb complement as needing 'to'
leaves the verb in its bare form after a preposition
mixes 'to' with the gerund, assuming the -ing form still needs a 'to' in front of it

items.sentence: That cough sounds bad — you ___ to see a doctor before it gets worse.

distractors.misconception: attaching 'to' to 'should' because 'ought to' has one, blending the two advice modals' patterns
assuming 'had better' takes 'to' like 'ought to' does
using a bare-verb obligation modal in a slot built for the to-pattern

items.sentence: I've checked the official timetable twice, so I'm completely sure: the last train ___ leave at exactly 11:40 tonight.

distractors.misconception: hedging with a weak-possibility modal despite the speaker's stated full certainty
presenting a verified scheduled fact as just one tentative possibility
defaulting to a polite weak-possibility modal for any statement about the future

items.sentence: The music is a bit too loud for the baby — could you turn it ___ a little?

distractors.misconception: confusing 'turn up' (increase the volume) with 'turn down' (decrease it)
confusing 'turn off' (switch off completely) with 'turn down' (reduce by a degree)
confusing 'turn over' (flip something / change TV channel) with volume control

items.sentence: My little brother isn't ___ to watch that horror movie yet.

distractors.misconception: placing 'enough' before the adjective on the model of 'too + adjective'
confusing 'too' (excess above the limit) with 'enough' (reaching the required level)
scrambling the word order and attaching 'too' after the adjective as if it worked like 'enough'

items.sentence: The doctor told him to drink ___ coffee and get more sleep.

distractors.misconception: hypercorrecting: applying the countable comparative to an uncountable substance noun
using the base countable quantifier instead of a comparative, and with the wrong noun type
confusing 'lesser' (lower in importance or rank) with 'less' (smaller quantity)

items.sentence: A: 'I've already seen that film twice.' B: '___ I — it's brilliant.'

distractors.misconception: treating 'So do I' as a frozen chunk instead of matching the auxiliary of the original statement
picking the right auxiliary but the wrong polarity for a positive statement
echoing a form of 'be' although the original statement contains no 'be' at all

items.sentence: Choose the most formal wording to ask a stranger at the bank: '___ I borrow your pen for a moment, please?'

distractors.misconception: treats 'can' as matching 'may' in formality when asking a stranger's permission
obligation read as formal permission
uses conditional 'would' with 'I' as if it formed a permission request

items.sentence: When the meeting ends, I ___ you my notes straight away.

distractors.misconception: present simple used for a one-off future act
uses past simple in the main clause for an event that is still in the future
treats a real future sequence as hypothetical or future-in-the-past

items.sentence: We ran into ____ at the market this morning, and she says hello.

distractors.misconception: drops the possessive 's after 'of' in the double genitive with a name
stacks the indefinite article directly onto a name's possessive, marking the noun twice
drops the indefinite article that the double genitive pattern requires

items.sentence: He's been really worried ____ his final exam results all week.

distractors.misconception: transfers 'with' from 'pleased with' to an emotion adjective that needs 'about'
borrows 'at' from surprise adjectives such as 'surprised at'
